source: Curated design-taste lessons for context-safe UI direction and visual assessment.
description: Human-scored scenarios for product-appropriate art direction, anti-default checks, implementation self-audits, and conditional browser visual assessment.

scenarios.prompt: Use b-design to create docs/DESIGN.md for a product with a public marketing page and a dense admin dashboard. The repository contains existing tokens, components, accessibility guidance, and a brand brief, but no named visual style. Before drafting the document, explain the design read, chosen art direction, and anti-default constraints for each surface. Keep local evidence authoritative and do not implement UI.
must: Make an explicit design read before drafting guidance, naming surface, audience, brand or repository evidence, hierarchy, density, layout variance, and motion posture
Choose a product-appropriate direction and anti-default constraints instead of applying one visual template to both surfaces
Preserve repository tokens and components and the docs/DESIGN.md-only scope
Keep any Mobbin use optional, bounded, and subordinate to local evidence
avoid: Apply a generic landing-page formula to the dashboard
Mandate a font, icon library, dark mode, image generation, or heavy motion without evidence
Choose the direction from personal taste while ignoring the repository or brand brief

scenarios.prompt: Use b-frontend to implement a scoped settings panel in an existing product app. The brief does not name an aesthetic; repository tokens and components plus an accessible trust-sensitive workflow are the authority. Before coding, state the design read and chosen product-appropriate direction with anti-default constraints. Then describe a preflight and self-audit across typography, palette, composition and layout repetition, surface and card restraint, meaningful interactions and states, truthful copy and assets, responsive behavior, and accessibility. Do not claim browser or visual proof.
must: Make the design read and chosen direction explicit before implementation
Use the existing stack and product context to choose hierarchy, density, composition, and motion
Self-audit typography, palette, composition or layout repetition, surfaces or cards, meaningful interactions, truthful copy or assets, responsive behavior, and accessibility
Keep browser or visual proof as a b-browser follow-up rather than claiming it from implementation work
avoid: Use a generic centered marketing hero, three equal feature cards, or unmotivated AI-purple gradients for the settings panel
Add speculative dependencies, external assets, fake data, or fabricated product claims
Claim visual or browser proof without real-browser evidence

scenarios.prompt: Use b-browser for a user-requested visual assessment of a responsive checkout flow. An approved brief and docs/DESIGN.md specify hierarchy, mobile composition, contrast and focus, and interaction affordances. Explain how you use them as the comparator, then collect the ordered browser evidence. Report concrete observations and gaps for hierarchy, clipping or overflow, responsive composition, contrast or focus or interaction affordance, and adherence to the specified design guidance. Explain what you would do if no approved comparator were supplied. Do not treat a generic page load or screenshot alone as aesthetic proof.
must: Make visual assessment conditional on the explicit request and the approved brief or design guidance
Compare concrete observable criteria including hierarchy, clipping or overflow, responsive composition, contrast or focus, interaction affordance, and adherence to specified guidance
Report observations and gaps rather than subjective aesthetic certification
Preserve the ordered browser evidence workflow and treat a screenshot as an artifact rather than proof by itself
avoid: Invent an aesthetic baseline when the approved comparator is missing
Claim visual quality from a generic page load or screenshot alone
Run a subjective visual assessment when it was not requested or no approved comparator exists
